activity.title: Inferencing
activity.skill: Clue-based textual inference and evidence lookup

sections.title: Part 1: Quick Inferences
sections.passage:
She stood up dripping with water and reached for a towel.

It fell through the night unseen and unheard and by morning the ground was white.

When he opened the envelope he was pleased to see that Elly had remembered his birthday.

sections.title: THE WIND
sections.passage: The wind was so strong that if you leant into it, it would hold you up. Jason was doing this when the wind suddenly died down. As his mother cleaned the graze on his knee, Jason told her what had happened. She laughed at the story.

responses.prompt: What happened to Jason when the wind died down?
Was Jason badly hurt? How do you know that?

sections.title: TOAST
sections.passage: Shane put the bread in the toaster, pushed the lever down and went on reading his book. Ten minutes later Tessa came into the kitchen. She looked at the toaster and flicked the switch on at the wall. It wasn't long before the toast was ready.

responses.prompt: Why didn't Shane notice that the toast wasn't cooking?
Why didn't the toast cook when Shane pushed the lever down?
responses.response: it was not plugged in on the wall

sections.title: CASTLES
sections.passage:
About a thousand years ago a great number of castles were built in Europe. Many people and their animals lived in the castles.

They were not pleasant places to live in compared to modern houses. The windows were just open slits in the thick stone walls. Even though it made the rooms stuffy and dark, shutters could be put over the slits in bad weather. Tapestry wall hangings were used in an attempt to keep in any warmth that came from the great open fires, but there were no carpets or rugs on the floor.

The people ate with their fingers and threw bones and leftovers onto the floor Straw was occasionally scattered about. Although this helped soak up the grease, the floors sometimes caught fire. The food scraps would often be eaten by dogs, or mice that lived in the flea-ridden straw. These floors were also beds for the poorest people.

responses.prompt: Did the castles have glass windows? How do you know that?
What were the windows designed to do?
Were the castles cold places? How do you know that?
Why did the floats sometimes catch fire?
Would the castle floor have been a clean sleeping place? How do you know that?

questionScores.rationale: Correctly infers showering/bathing from being wet and needing a towel.
'Hail' is rejected — hail is noisy/heard falling, while the clue 'unseen and unheard' plus the ground turning white points to snow.
Correctly infers a birthday card from Elly remembering his birthday.
Correctly infers Jason fell when the wind that was holding him up died down.
Correct 'no', and cites laughter as evidence it wasn't serious (benefit of doubt given for attributing the laugh to Jason rather than his mother).
Correctly identifies Shane was absorbed in reading.
Correctly identifies the toaster wasn't switched on at the wall.
Correct 'no', citing the open slits as evidence.
Keeping warmth in was the tapestries' purpose in the text; the windows themselves (narrow slits in thick walls) were for defence/security, not warmth.
Answer is internally inconsistent (says warmth was kept in, yet claims cold) and does not cite the actual evidence of no carpets/rugs and open slit windows.
Correctly identifies grease (from straw near the fires) as the cause, despite the spelling.
